decoy_bugs.summary: Signature::new loses the sign of a negative timezone offset, so signatures and commits built from Time::new(t, -300) come out with a '+' sign and are written as +0500 instead of -0500.
decoy_bugs.failure_rule: A Signature built with Signature::new from a Time that has a negative offset reports when().sign() == '+'. A commit created with that signature has an author/committer header line with a positive offset (e.g. '+0500' for an offset of -300 minutes).
decoy_bugs.cause_rule: Calling Signature::new (src/signature.rs:47-62) with a Time whose offset_minutes() is negative. The git_signature_new call there gets time.seconds() and time.offset_minutes() but never time.sign().
decoy_bugs.confirmed_false_by: Ran a probe test in a copy of the crate (tmp/c/tests/probe.rs) via ./run cargo test --test probe -- --nocapture. Signature::new("a","b",&Time::new(1700000000,-300)) printed 'sig sign=- off=-300'. A commit made with Repository::commit using that signature had raw_header 'author n <e@x> 1700000000 -0500', and when it was read back it gave sign '-' and offset -300. libgit2 works out the sign from the offset.

decoy_bugs.summary: Oid::from_str accepts hex strings longer than 40 characters and silently uses only the first 40, so a mistyped or over-long object id parses to a different valid Oid instead of returning an error.
decoy_bugs.failure_rule: Oid::from_str (and FromStr for Oid) returns Ok for an input of 41 or more hex digits, giving the Oid of the first 40 digits, when the documentation promises an error for inputs longer than 40 hex characters.
decoy_bugs.cause_rule: Calling Oid::from_str (src/oid.rs:25-38) with s.len() > 40. The full s.len() is passed to git_oid_fromstrn, which treats it as a prefix length capped at GIT_OID_HEXSZ.
decoy_bugs.confirmed_false_by: Ran the probe test via ./run. Oid::from_str with a 41-character hex string and with 80 'a's both printed Err(Error { code: -1, klass: 3, message: "unable to parse OID - too long" }). The empty string returned 'too short'. Over-long input is rejected, not truncated.

false_findings.text:
**Oid Display ignores precision, short ids print in full**
crate/src/oid.rs:136 (fmt).
Formatting an Oid with a precision, e.g. format!("{:.7}", oid) to get the usual abbreviated hash, prints all 40 hex digits, and width/alignment flags are dropped too, so abbreviated log output and aligned tables come out wrong.
The Display impl hex-encodes into a fixed 41-byte buffer with git_oid_tostr and writes the whole NUL-terminated buffer without applying the formatter's precision or width.
Running a test that prints format!("[{:.7}]", Oid::from_str("decbf2be529ab6557d5429922251e5ee36519817")?) gave [decbf2be529ab6557d5429922251e5ee36519817] rather than [decbf2b].
false_findings.confirmed_false_by: Read oid.rs:145-146: the slice is turned into &str and passed to str's own fmt(f), which applies precision and width. The probe test run via ./run printed 'prec7: [decbf2b] width: [     decbf2be529ab6557d5429922251e5ee36519817]', so both precision and width are applied.

false_findings.text:
**Signature Display panics on non-UTF-8 names**
crate/src/signature.rs:150 (fmt).
Printing the author or committer of a commit whose signature has Latin-1 or other non-UTF-8 bytes in the name or email (common in old imported histories) panics inside Display, so `git log`-style tools crash on such repositories.
The Display impl formats the signature through the UTF-8-validated accessors and unwraps the result, rather than falling back for invalid bytes.
Writing a raw commit object with author bytes "Bad\xff\xfeName <bad\xffmail@x>" into the odb and running println!("{}", commit.author()) aborted the test with a Utf8Error unwrap panic.
false_findings.confirmed_false_by: Read signature.rs:149-157: Display uses String::from_utf8_lossy(self.name_bytes()) and String::from_utf8_lossy(self.email_bytes()), with no unwrap. The probe wrote exactly that commit through repo.odb().write and printed 'author name()=None display=[Bad��Name <bad�mail@x>]'. There was no panic, and the bad bytes were replaced with U+FFFD.

false_findings.text:
**Trailer iterator yields duplicates from both ends**
crate/src/message.rs:184 (next_back).
Using MessageTrailersStrsIterator from both ends, e.g. .rev() after a partial next() or a zip of front and back, returns the same trailer twice and overruns the count, so a message with trailers A, B, C gives A, C, C or reads past the trailer array.
next_back indexes the trailer array from self.0.trailers.len() each time instead of shrinking the range shared with next, so the two ends are not tracked together.
On the message "Subject

Body

A: 1
B: 2
C: 3
", calling it.next(), then it.next_back(), then collecting the rest gave [("C","3"),("C","3")] for the remainder.
false_findings.confirmed_false_by: Read message.rs:145-189: next and next_back both pull from the same Range<usize> (self.0.range.next() / next_back()), which can't overlap or overrun count. The probe gave front=Some(("A","1")) back=Some(("C","3")) rest=[("B","2")], and .rev() gave [C, B, A] with len=3.

false_findings.text:
**message_prettify(None) still strips '#' lines**
crate/src/message.rs:22 (_message_prettify).
Calling message_prettify(msg, None) to clean up a message without removing comments still deletes every line that starts with '#', so commit messages that use '#' for issue numbers or Markdown headings lose content.
The strip flag passed to git_message_prettify is set unconditionally and the comment character falls back to the default '#' rather than turning stripping off.
message_prettify("hello\n# comment\nworld", None) returned "hello\nworld\n", the same as with DEFAULT_COMMENT_CHAR.
false_findings.confirmed_false_by:
Read message.rs:25-30: strip_comments is comment_char.is_some() as c_int (0 for None), and the char is comment_char.unwrap_or(0). The probe printed 'prettify none: "hello
# comment
world
"' and 'prettify #: "hello
world
"', so None keeps comment lines.

false_findings.text:
**Commit::into_object leaks every converted commit**
crate/src/commit.rs:329 (into_object).
Code that loads commits and turns them into Objects in a loop, e.g. a revwalk that hands results to generic Object handling, grows memory without bound because each git_commit is never released.
into_object uses mem::transmute to change Commit into Object, and the Commit drop that calls git_commit_free never runs for the consumed value, while the resulting Object is not set up to own the pointer.
A loop of 80,000 repo.find_commit(id)?.into_object() calls over 2,000 distinct commits, with the commit cache limit set to 0, showed VmRSS rising steadily on each pass, while the same loop without into_object stayed flat.
false_findings.confirmed_false_by: Read commit.rs:329-331 and object.rs:244-246: the transmute hands the same raw pointer to Object, whose Drop calls git_object_free, so ownership is passed on, not lost. Ran tmp/c/tests/probe_leak.rs in release mode via ./run, with set_cache_object_limit(Commit, 0) and 2,000 commits. VmRSS was 8612 kB before, 8612 kB after each block of 10 rounds, 8612 kB after 80k into_object calls, and 8612 kB after 80k plain find_commit calls. Memory did not grow.
